utterances.text: Okay. So, in other words, you are also not including here the situations or events in 2001 where members of the army, such as in Radusa, had to undertake, shall we say, defensive actions?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And isn't it also true, though, if we're talking about a crisis that stretched from approximately February to August, so about seven months, that six combat operations is actually quite a bit, isn't it? Six combat planned -- excuse me. Five combat operations carried out by the armed forces in seven months. Isn't that quite a bit?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely no. I don't see where you draw this conclusion or where this logic comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a period of a single month, if we are discussing dealing with terrorist organisations one might have even 30 different activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, in 2001, as you point out in your report, the security forces were having trouble mobilising sufficient personnel. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so it wasn't always so easy for the security forces to mount an operation, was it, an offensive operation?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the problems with the personnel?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For example, yes.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both yes and no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, can you think of -- correct me if I'm wrong, Macedonia became a republic in 1991 or 1992? Which year was it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can you --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first constitution has been passed on the 17th of November, 1991, for the independent and sovereign Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you think of any year prior to 2001, when -- can you think of any year between 1991 up through the year 2000 when the army of the Republic of Macedonia was ordered to undertake six combat operations and actually undertook five of them?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until 2000, there was no such case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can we turn, please, to paragraph 181 of your report, please.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you say it well, because 181 does not exist in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Really? I have it here. I may be reading an older version.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I submitted certain changes and amendments to the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to find it right now. You're probably right. All right. If 181 has been removed, then I'm not going to ask you about it. And it has been.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's -- for the first time, maybe you can agree with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Oh, it's not the first time. All right. Would you agree with me that during 2001, a division developed, if I can call it that, between President Trajkovski, who, as Supreme Commander, commanded the army, and Prime Minister Georgievski because the prime minister, according to the constitution, could command the units of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes there were certain disagreements between the president and Supreme Commander of the armed forces and the prime minister, and I responded to one of the questions of the Defence. I said that when the issue was whether to accept such an idea for declaration of a state of war, the president was against it and the prime minister was in favour. This is at least according to the information I've got.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, my colleague is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to object to a portion of the question on page 48, line 3, where it says that the prime minister according to the constitution could have had command of the police forces. I think that this is an incorrect assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's noted, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: These disagreements between the president and the prime minister, didn't they also, at times, lead to problems or disagreements during joint operations between the police -- involving the police and the army?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are discussing here a different point of view, how to deal with the crisis back in 2001. These are ideas, positions of certain individuals. In this particular case, one of the highest ranking officials and the most responsible ones. However, the army, nor the police depend on the position of the prime minister or the president, but they depend on the constitution and the legal provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So did I take your response as a yes or a no?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They do not depend on the personal opinions of anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, that's -- that may be true.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite sure it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Fine. I'll use your words. I'm sure it's true, but it can happen, can't it, that the positions of people in power can have -- positions of people in leadership roles can have an influence or effect on their subordinates, can't it? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. These are their political positions which are limited by the constitutions -- constitution and the laws. Outside the law and the constitution, the president cannot act, nor the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But within the law and the constitution, in 2001, the prime minister, through the minister of the interior, could exert some influence on the activities of the Ministry of Interior and the police, couldn't he?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense are you referring to? If you're talking in the sense of the engagement of the police, I would be able to provide an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I believe you say at several points in your report. In fact, let's take a look at paragraph 216. Hopefully this paragraph still exists.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Now, for example, the start of paragraph 16 [sic] the government -- at least this is the English translation so if there's a problem with the translation, you correct me, okay? "The government has authority over the structures of the police."

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, which article or which paragraph are we discussing?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Paragraph 216.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Again, I was trying to avoid any mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's fine. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Paragraph 216 begins like this: "The government has authority over the structures of the police. The prime minister of the Republic of Macedonia commands the units of the Ministry of Interior and does so through the minister of the interior, i.e., through the director of the security and counter-intelligence office." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And later on you quote a particular plan for the use of the security forces, which states that: "The command of the units of the Ministry of Interior falls within the competence of the prime minister of the Republic of Macedonia, through the minister of the interior." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, wouldn't it be fair, then, to say that during the crisis time in 2001, the prime minister, through the minister of the interior, could exercise, at a minimum could exercise some influence over the units of the Ministry of Interior? You yourself say he could command them.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister, in the sense of using the forces. The prime minister, referring their use. Yes, he could have had a certain influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And if that's the case, and since the prime minister and the president disagreed on how to deal with the crisis in 2001, didn't the prime minister's views sometimes affect how joint operations were planned and carried out?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to answer by using a military term. When certain competencies are given to a major or a general, having in mind their rank, the last say is given by the general. In this particular case, the last say goes to the president and the Supreme Commander of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. While we're on paragraph 216, there's something I want to ask you about. We've just seen it a minute ago. At the beginning of paragraph 216, you say that: "The prime minister of the Republic of Macedonia commands the units of the Ministry of Interior and does so through the minister of the interior, i.e., through the director of the security and counter-intelligence office." Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then you say: "Confirmation of this is item 17 of the plan for the use of the security forces of the Republic of Macedonia." All right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One has to continue: "Related to the resolution of the crisis in 2001."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show the witness what is 65 ter 700, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Dr. Markovski, this is at tab 52 in the second binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If the usher could help you by making sure you have binder number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in e-court, could we please turn to the very last page in both versions. I'd like you to focus on Article 17, which is what you refer to in paragraph 216 for your report. Now you can certainly tell me whether there's a problem with the English translation in Article 17, Dr. Markovski. But Article 17 in English says this: "The commands over the units of the Ministry of Internal Affairs is under the competence of the president of the government of the Republic of Macedonia, through the minister of internal affairs?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what the document reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: There's no reference to the sector for security and counter-intelligence, is there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here in this Article, it is obviously missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, we're looking at it in English and Macedonian. This is what you cited to in your report, 65 ter 700.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you need to have something in mind, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That this document, which we are reviewing now, and which bears the title: Plan on use the security forces of the Republic of Macedonia, stems from the plan of the president to deal with the crisis in 2001. That plan was revealed by the president on a special session of the parliament of the Republic of Macedonia, on the 6th -- on the 8th of June, I apologise. 8th of June, the government fully supported it, this plan, and undertook the obligation to make this plan operational, in coordination and conjunction with the president. While the crisis body that was activated at that moment and where members were in addition to certain responsible structures and members of the ministries from the Republic of Macedonia by also representatives of the NATO, KFOR, OSCE, the European Union, et cetera, representatives of several diplomatic bodies in the Republic of Macedonia, it prepared this version and then as a document of the government of the Republic of Macedonia, it was aligned for implementation and was implemented as planned here. I see no possibility for discrepancies in terms of implementation of this plan between the president, as the Supreme Commander of the armed forces, and the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just for the record, Your Honour, last week I asked my colleagues from the Defence of Mr. Tarculovski for a copy of this plan. Because it is mentioned at least in one point somewhere else in this expert report but to date the Prosecution hasn't received it. I'm going to move on. Your Honour, Ms. Residovic is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I noticed that. Yes, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours if I may be of assistance. This document is Exhibit 1D177.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that. I don't think that is mentioned in the expert report, so I didn't know that until just now. And it is not cited to in paragraph 216 either. Can we turn back, please -- can we go back to paragraph 202, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And paragraph 202, you describe the new Law on Defence. And you say: The new law was compatible with the strategic aims of the state for the transformation of the defence and was not in any way connected to the situation. When you say "was not in any way connected to the situation," are you saying the passage of the new Law on Defence was not in any way connected to the crisis in 2001?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reason for the adoption of this law or to amend the old law was the transformation, the need of transformation of the Defence according with the NATO standard and in line with the proposal made by representatives of the friendly countries, the ministries of countries friendly to the Republic of Macedonia which suggested that the sector of defence needs to undergo a larger transformation, so this is the sense in which I am speaking that this law stemmed from the need to transform the defence sector particularly the army structure and not because of the situation current at that time. Even if that situation did not exist, a new law would have been adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And in the last sentence of paragraph 202 -- first of all, you talk about in paragraph 202, you talk about the necessity of passing regulations or by-laws and that the old law would be applied until the passing of the by-laws for the new law, right? And then you say in the last sentence: "During the crisis, this was especially characteristic with relation to the competencies of the president of the Republic of Macedonia regarding the command of the army and the issuing of tasks and duties to the police forces." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, you refer to the president's command over the army and to the president's issuing of tasks and duties to the police forces.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you do that, because under the old law, without a state of war declared, the president could command the army but not the police. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I wish to point out here actually through this position that I have presented, is that even without the state of war having been declared, the president, probably due to reasons known to himself only, in certain situations actually acted as if he had commanded the police and the army in circumstances of war. Why did he do that, I don't know. I'm making a conclusion that did he so. In my assessment, it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, you're a political/military expert here, Dr. Markovski. Isn't it true that the reason the president acted as if he had commanded the police and the army in circumstances of war, even without a declaration of a state of war, it's because, de facto, Macedonia was in a state of war. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That is not right. The Republic of Macedonia was not in a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, can we turn, please, to what is 65 ter 644. And, Your Honours, this will be at tab 49 in binder 2 of the documents that have you with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you can take a look at this document, please, it's dated the 3rd of May, 2001, and it's a decision by President Trajkovski, entitled the use of the army of the Republic of Macedonia to carry out an operation? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the president refers to Article 79 of the constitution and Article 15 of the Law on Defence. And then he says -- his decision say this is, and in paragraph 1: "The army of the Republic of Macedonia, in cooperation with the forces of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, to carry out an operation to destroy the terrorist forces in the wider region of the villages Vaksince and Slupcane, and in the other areas within the zones of responsibilities where diversion terrorist groups appear?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we scroll down in English please so we can see the bottom of page. And we see it is submitted to the cabinet of the president and to the General Staff of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, the best that the president could do at that time was to seek the police's cooperation, isn't that true, with the army? He could not order the police to act. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You are not understanding this correctly. What I mean is I don't wish to offend you, but this is not what it reads here, what is the substance of this decision. Here we can find two key points. The first one is what I'm asserting as well, that in the Republic of Macedonia in 2001 there was no state of war. This decision is a result of the emergence of the need to carry out an operation to destroy the terrorist forces. We are not speaking about armed forces. We are speaking about terrorist forces. And the second one present here and this is how the first time item starts, the army of the Republic of Macedonia, in conjunction with the MOI forces should carry out this operation. This mean, at the same time, a task for both the army and the Ministry of Interior, where such joint activities are carried out of the security forces, which would mean of the army and of the police forces from the Ministry of the Interior command belongs to a military officer. This is why the president forwards this decision to the General Staff of the army of the Republic of Macedonia, which should make this decision operational, and detail the obligations, the duties for both the army and the police forces that will carry out there operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And he couldn't forward this to the prime minister because he could not -- the president could not forward such a decision to the prime minister because the prime minister controlled the forces of the Ministry of Interior. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had no obligation to forward it there. It was sufficient to sent it to the General Staff of the army, and the General Staff of the army will make the task operational and issue all tasks to all participants in this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can I ask the interpreter, please to read the first line of paragraph 1, please, to read it in English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The army of the Republic of Macedonia, in cooperation with the forces of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, to carry out an operation to destroy the territory forces in the wider region of the villages of Vaksince and Slupcane and in the other areas within the zone of responsibility where diversion terrorist groups appear. The interpreter is not sure what the request was. I'm reading the first paragraph in the English translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Interpreter, that's fine, and I simply wanted to see whether our CLSS interpreters interpretation would match the written translation and it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I believe the interpreter said she was reading from the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then -- then I was not clear. I was asking the interpreter to -- I meant -- the interpreter to read from -- to interpret the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And were you wanting just a sentence or a paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The first line of the Macedonian version, please if that could be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter just needs a moment to read the sentence before interpreting it. "The army of the Republic of Macedonia in conjunction with the MOI forces to carry out an operation to destroy the terrorist forces in the boarder regions of villages Vaksince and Slupcane --"

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's fine. Okay, well then we stand corrected. There's a problem with the translation. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours because the interpreter already interpreted it, we believe that it would be co-action, but yes conjunction works fine. This is the first things we wish to react about, and second thing is the 65 ter 644 that my learned colleague cites to is it Exhibit 1D50.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that. It is referred to 65 ter 644 in Dr. Markovski's report, and I'm simply using the authorities cited in Dr. Markovski's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can turn, please, to paragraph 206 of your report, Dr. Markovski. And in paragraph 206, you talk about the system of command within the army of the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then you -- in paragraph 207 you refer to Article 12 of the Law on Army Service. And then in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Saxon, I entered corrections here and amendments that it was not Article 12 of the Law on Service in the army but Article 28 on the Law on Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the same will apply to 28 in the final sentence. So 208 in the final sentence. It is again Article 28 of Law on Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And focussing now for a moment on paragraph 208 you say: "The regulation of the Law on Defence connected to the subject of this report was practically applied when the president gave a direct order by way of telephone to Major Despodov on the completion of tasks related to Ljuboten. Then you say: "Major Despodov --" [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I make it clear there is a button on my desk which is very awkwardly placed, and if it is lent on by the weight of a pad, it will often switch off the microphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's all right, Your Honour, I have many awkward things in my life too. So I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The last and then -- in the end of paragraph 208, you say: "Major Despodov, pursuant to his own duties specified in the Law on Defence -- Article 28, was obligated to execute it," referring to the direct order of the president. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes it is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then you cite para 2 in footnote 118, you cite to a report by -- by Captain Ljupco Kostadinov on the 12th of August, 2001, which is Exhibit P303. Now, when you cited to this report, were you also citing to it as authority for your statement that the president gave a direct order by telephone to Major Despodov?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but probably it was so, because my point is that the president has such right and has directly issued an order to Major Despodov.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can we show the witness what is Exhibit P103, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this is in your -- this is in your fourth -- I was about to misspeak. Your Honours, this is in binder 2, tab number 53.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And could the witness be assisted so that he has the hard copy in front of him, please, because that might speed this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It should be Exhibit P303. I apologise. And this should be at tab number 53 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Dr. Markovski, where in this report do you find the president of Macedonia issuing a direct order to Major Despodov?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the English version is not here in the binder, so allow me to read this document from the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, I'll give you my copy. I'll give you my copy in Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could the usher assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is in the first paragraph of page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Can we turn to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you read the sentence where it indicates for you that Major Despodov received a direct order from the president.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Around 1800 to 1900 hours first a person Johan talked to the president of the state and then Major Despodov personally talked with the president. The president asked him whether he was under the command of General Sokol. Major Despodov answered yes. The president told him, good I will talk to General Sokol, and I will call you again." Which means this conversation took place on the basis of the fact that Major Despodov had prior opportunity to talk to the president, to receive an order from him and probably to ask that this is done to request that this order is also notified of Mr. -- of General Sokol Mitrevski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, there's nothing in what you've just read that indicates that the president gave a direct order to Major Despodov, is there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there are other documents which corroborate the notion that the president has, indeed, given an order. Primarily the report of the Despodov's superior, the commander of the 1st Guardist Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see, Dr. Markovski, the difficulty is that the only thing you cited to in footnote 118 is this particular document, Exhibit P303. You didn't cite to other documents.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. I probably considered that this was a sufficient corroboration or support for my statement, but I'm saying now that there are other documents and that report also of the command of the 1st Guardist Brigade is available. Have you it. But I really can't give you anymore specific help at the time moment. I don't know what the specific number of it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. Would this be the right time for the second break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Indeed, it is. We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we can show the witness what is Exhibit P91, the constitution of the Republic of Macedonia, please. This is tab -- at tab 51 in the second Prosecution binder. And, first of all, if we can turn to what is Article 79 for a moment, please, which in the English version is at ERN N001-8982.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, Dr. Markovski, Article 79 has three provisions of it. Paragraph 1 says -- I'm sorry, are you with me? Do you have Article 79?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph 1 says: "The president of the Republic of Macedonia represents the Republic." Paragraph 2 says: "The president of the Republic is Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces of Macedonia." Paragraph 3 says: "The president of the Republic exercises his or her rights and duties on the basis and within the framework of the constitution and laws." You followed with me?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn now to Article 124, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we've seen this before, of course. Article 124 describes a state of war. It says: "A state of war exists within direct danger of military attack on the Republic is impending or when the Republic is attacked or war is declared on it." And then paragraphs 2 and 3 describe how a state of war may be declared and under what circumstances. I'm just trying to understand. Yesterday, I believe it was in response to some questions from my colleague Ms. Residovic. You explained that in issuing orders to the army and the police or to the army and then through the army to the police, the president relied on Article 79 of the constitution for doing that. And we even saw the references to Article 79 in several of the orders or decisions issued by the president. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And more precisely, Article 79, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And Article 79, paragraph 2, says that the president of the Republic is Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces of Macedonia, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But without the declaration of a state of war, how would Article 79, subparagraph 2, give powers to the president over the police?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that in certain situations, the president behaved as if it was state of war and why did he do so and where he draw his powers from, I cannot really comment on. I was just explaining the facts of the situation, and it is obvious from these orders, and one of those we saw it a bit earlier and we discussed it and we could see that the army is going to perform these duties in co-action with the police; it was a joint activity by both armed forces and why the president behaved in this manner, I'm not capable of explaining this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Just so that I understand then, your testimony and the circumstances of 2001, although a state of war was not declared, the president behaved as if a state of war had been declared. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain circumstances, yes. I would add, in certain circumstances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And although a state of war had not been declared, the president asserted certain powers as if a state of war had been declared. Is that -- in certain circumstances. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could accept this kind of assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. But wouldn't it be fair to say, that because a state of war had not been declared and in certain circumstances the president acted as if a state of war had been declared, that, in a sense, the president was acting, if you will forgive the expression, sort of inside a legal vacuum?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you're completely right here, because in 2001 the Republic of Macedonia, as a young democracy did not have developed all the procedures with respect to situation of crisis. Mainly I refer to the fact that Macedonia, only in 2005, adopted the Law on Crisis Management or the Law on Management of Crisis and in this period if such a law would have existed probably the president and everyone else involved, in accordance with this law, they would conduct their activities pursuant to the provisions of this law. At that time, crisis management law did not exist and the crisis management body, the precise title was coordinative body for crisis management established by the government, I could not find corroboration on which basis it has been organised. Probably the situation was such that such a body was required, but I could not find a special regulation that would point out to the establishment and activity an organisation of this body. So this cannot be found in any of the regulations of that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can show the witness what is now Exhibit P606.1, please. That is the more complete version of the old Law on Defence that was admitted this morning. And we need to look at Article 15, please. So if we could turn to the next page in the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the counsel to adjust the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sorry about that. Thank you. And if we could go to Article 15 in the English version as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see that in the old Law on Defence, the president of the Republic, under Article 15, subparagraph 12: "Commands the use of the police for execution of combat tasks in a state of war." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, of course, as we know --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn, please, to Article 23. Probably the next page in Macedonian and one or two more pages in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in Article 23 of the old Law on Defence, we see that in a state of war, the police may be used in order to perform combat tasks as an integral part of the army. You see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what it reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, of course, we know that during the crisis time in 2001, no state of war was ever declared, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It appears there is a technical problem with the transcript. We will wait a little while and it may be able to be restored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, it appears that the technical problem is resolved. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We've just looked at Article 23 of the old Law on Defence. And we've just reminded ourselves that in 2001 a state of war was not declared. If we could turn to what is Exhibit 1D0098, please, which is the new Law on Defence that was enacted in 2001. It's at tab 48 of the second binder. And first if we could look at what is Article 24, please. That has ERN number N002-2795 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this chapter, chapter 4 of the 2001 law, Dr. Markovski, refers to the armed forces of the Republic of Macedonia, and in Article 24 it begins: "The armed forces structure elements are: Unit, commands, staffs, and institutions." And then a couple of lines below that in the English version, it says: "The armed forces consists of services, branches and technical services." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can accept it as correct, but the mistake is not of an essential importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is, again, a mistake in the translation. In the Macedonian text it reads army and in the English version we have armed forces. We are discussing Article 24 that was cited by my learned colleague right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well then I need to seek some clarification from Dr. Markovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This chapter on the armed forces of the Republic of Macedonia, Article 22, refers to the "armed forces are the armed force of all citizens of the Republic. There are active forces and reserve forces." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 24, exclusively refers to the army and not to the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I know that, Dr. Markovski. But I just asked you a question about Article 22. Article 22 refers to the armed forces. Is that right? Or do we have another translation problem?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see Article 22 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we see the previous page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please go back a page.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please continue with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Does Article 22 refer just to the army or does it refer to the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here the army is a synonym of the armed forces as it is represented in Article 22 as an armed force of all the citizens of the Republic. And it is composed of the regular and reserve forces. Article 24 exclusively mentioned the army, but this is not an essential problem whether we have to understand the army as an armed force or just as an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. As you -- as you mention, Article 24 refers expressly to the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are not always able to follow the translation of this document but the whole chapter, chapter number 4 the title is army of the Republic of Macedonia, and the translated document reads armed forces of the Republic of Macedonia and this is not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, with that correction that will probably shorten some of my questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber, though, would ask you to have the translation checked with the translation service of chapter 4 and the references whether it to be army or armed forces, because if it is simply referring to army, there are some grammatical problems in the translation of particular articles. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I can intervene, maybe I can help out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, I think we leave it to Mr. Saxon and the appropriate translators. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to Article 172, one of the last Articles of this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And -- I'm sorry, if we could focus on Article 174. It's on the same page. And it says: "This Law --" I don't know what is going on in the Macedonian version. We just need to stop right there?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "This Law comes into effect from the eighth day from its publication in the official register in the Republic of Macedonia." Do you see that, Dr. Markovski?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it. This is what it reads and this is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this law was published in the Official Gazette on the 8th [sic] of June, 2001, so its effective date then would have been the 9th of June, 2001. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be precise about this. I have never thought about this problem. In my opinion - just a moment, please - yes, this is how it should be, as you interpreted it. This is how I understand it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Now hypothetically speaking if a few days after the 9th of June 2001 the president of the Republic of Macedonia had issued an order which was based --

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not receive interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you hear me now? Okay. If hypothetically the president of the Republic of Macedonia had issued an order a few days after the 9th of June, which was based on this law, that would be an indication that this law had come into effect, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, I would refer you to what is Exhibit 1D00060.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And before we loose it on the screen, lines 15, 16, 17 of page 3, are you saying that the Gazettel was on the 8th of June or the 1st of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my understanding it was on the 1st of June. We can certainly go back to the first page and check it in the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It just appears in line 15 as the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That I believe is an error, probably my error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So the line 16 would then be correct if the 1st of June was the correct date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Moving to another topic, can you turn, please, to your expert report, Dr. Markovski, paragraph 239. And in paragraph 239, you talk about units of movements of organised resistance --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can counsel please turn on his mic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the end of paragraph 239, you explain that units of movements of organised resistance that belong to a warring faction are also considered to be part of the armed forces, regardless of whether they are at war on domestic, foreign, occupied, or unoccupied territory on the following conditions. And then you list four conditions there. You see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the first condition is that their members are organised militarily (have a leader that is responsible for his subordinates). Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we show Dr. Markovski what is Exhibit P321, please. And this is a document known as the NATO briefing pack. And Your Honours can find it at tab 36 of the first binder. And it might be easier if Dr. Markovski could be given the first binder so he could look at the hard copy as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat, which tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Tab 36 of the first binder. And you should have a copy there in English and in Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Before we discuss the document, you refer -- you rely on this document in your report in a number of footnotes. You cite to this document at footnote 18, 39, 42 through 44, and footnote 65. Since you rely on this document to that degree, do you accept that the information in it is correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I find them correct but considering that this is an international factor, they're respectable information I appreciate those. I can't say whether they are accurate or not, but I appreciate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn please to the page that has ERN number R037-6858.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, for example, this page describes the NLA military structure. Do you see that, Dr. Markovski?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The diagram of the so-called NLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we go two pages further on. It has ERN number R037-6860, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on this page we see the NLA military command. Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm following you. It says political speaker of the NLA, Ali Ahmeti, Abazi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And below Ali Ahmeti we see Gzim Ostreni, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And if we can just move one page further along to ERN number R037-6861. Here we see a description of the NLA military command and the brigades. Do you see that, Dr. Markovski?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So at least in the viewpoint of NATO, the NLA had an organised military structure, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it is insufficient to look at these diagrams only. We should read the narrative part as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm asking to you look at these diagrams and tell me whether, in the viewpoint of NATO, the NLA had an organised military structure?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything until we corroborate this by narrative part as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Markovski, if we could turn then to what is ERN R037-6866, please. Dr. Markovski, this is the only narrative text that talks about some of the NLA personalities. You see Gzim, Plaku, Ostreni, at the top, and if you follow the asterisk, there is some description of his particulars in the middle of the page. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now this is the only narrative text that this document contains regarding NLA personalities. But would this help you to agree that in NATO's view, the NLA had a military structure?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we have here is depictions in the first place of Ali Ahmeti as the political spokesperson, not the Supreme Commander or any other office. Gzim, Plaku, Ostreni is shown here as Chief of Staff of Ona, not chief of General Staff of Ona -- of NLA. And no numbers are given with regards to these squares that are indicated as brigades. So from this aspect, we should approach with doubt the qualification whether this is some armed group within a given region, or whether it is really a brigade, particularly since there is no document related to any of these brigades anywhere here, a document which would really corroborate the notion that those are brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So the answer to your question [sic] -- excuse me, the answer to my question would be no, right?

utterances.speaker: BLAGOJA MARKOVSKI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said at the beginning, these documents I find respectable but it does not give me right to assert that the NLA was an organised armed structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Apostolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, but could my learned colleague from the Prosecutor's office tell the expert what was the NATO source for this information, so maybe the expert would be able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I find that irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think, Mr. Apostolski, we can leave Mr. Saxon to develop his questions. If you think it, in the end, is going to be material, your re-examination can deal with that. And we have come our allotted time, I'm afraid, Mr. Saxon. So we must adjourn for the day, to resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of March, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
